Start with **one click per test**; two is a bigger step if one click produces almost no feel change. Fewer clicks out from fully clockwise (stiff) adds damping; more clicks out softens it. What are you trying to improve—harshness, dive, kicking, or something else?

The cold-to-hot change points first to damping fade: as shock oil heats, it thins and the damping weakens, so the rear can feel softer and return too quickly. A rough engineering estimate for typical 5W suspension oil is about 38% thinner across a 60–95°F air-temperature change; the actual change depends on the oil and shock temperature. A leak, low gas charge, or worn internal parts are other possibilities. With the bike off and cool, look for fresh oil on the shock and visible damage around the shock or linkage, then have a suspension shop assess the shock hot and cold. Don’t ride it if it’s leaking or the rear feels unstable.
A shock that turns soft and bouncy only after 20 minutes most likely has heat-related damping fade. Don’t tune around it with clickers; have the shock checked before riding hard again.

For routine maintenance, use the guided job **“Release built-up air from the fork and clean the dust boots.”** Start with the fork cold, before riding: record how it felt last ride, put the bike on a lift stand with the front wheel off the ground, then open each top bleeder screw to release pressure and close it again. The job then covers removing the protectors, cleaning and lightly oiling the dust boots and tubes, and refitting everything; keep oil off the brake disc. You’ll need a lift stand, a screwdriver or bit, clean rags and universal oil spray. Tap **“Working on the bike?”** to start it; I can walk you through those steps here too.

That routine is not an internal air-chamber rebuild: the available job excludes air-pressure setting, oil changes and seal replacement. For internal AER chamber disassembly or seal service, follow the suspension service procedure for this fork (GASGAS's spec) or have a suspension shop handle it. If you’re only resetting pressure afterward, the stock setting is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**. Oil on the inner tubes or dripping from a dust boot means have the seals checked before riding.
Routine external AER maintenance is bleeding the cold fork and cleaning the dust boots; internal air-chamber service is a separate job. GASGAS calls for fork service once after 10 operating hours, then every 40 hours.

A clean, dry shock isn’t proof it’s healthy—look for fresh oil around the shaft or body, and note damping that fades late in a moto, inconsistent return, or a rear end that starts kicking or packing without a setup change. Those symptoms can also come from linkage, bearings, or setup, so they don’t prove the shock itself needs a rebuild. Have a suspension shop assess it if it’s due or showing symptoms; the shock is pressurized. If oil is reaching the tire or brake, don’t ride it.

A **revalve changes the internal shim stack and damping flow**, so the tuner can reshape how the fork or shock resists movement at different shaft speeds and through the stroke. The clickers adjust the existing valve’s external bleed or needle setting; they can fine-tune it, but they can’t make a mismatched internal damping curve behave like a different one.

That’s why clickers can reach a point where softer helps one part of the track but leaves another unsupported—or firmer helps bottoming but makes small bumps harsh. A revalve can target that compromise. It doesn’t change the spring rate: get spring and sag right first, then consider valving if the clickers can’t cover the track and feel you want.
A revalve changes the suspension’s internal damping curve; clickers only adjust the range the existing internals provide. Springs and sag still need to suit your weight before valving is the answer.

Your 2023 MC 250F has a WP XACT AER air fork; GasGas’s published stock air pressure is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**. Inside, the air chamber replaces the coil spring: pressure sets support and acts progressively as the fork compresses, while a coil fork gets its spring force from the steel spring and changing the rate means changing springs. In either design, damping—not the spring—controls the fork’s compression and return speed. The air fork is easier to tune for support with pressure, but pressure must be checked; a coil fork is simpler to set and doesn’t need an air-pressure check.

Separate safety note: the 2023 MC 250F is among the GasGas models named in the front-caliper recall; have a dealer confirm whether the remedy has been completed.
An air fork uses compressed air as its spring; a spring fork uses a steel coil. Both still use oil damping to control how quickly the fork moves.
